title: The Fire Triangle
description: Heat, fuel and air, why wood never burns directly, and the ten minutes before you strike
tryIt: With an adult nearby, blow out a candle gently and relight it by holding a lit match in its rising smoke a few centimetres above the wick, as Faraday did.

concepts.title: How it works: heat, fuel and air
concepts.contentHtml:
It is getting dark, the wind is rising and you have one match. Before you strike it, it helps to know what a fire actually is, because that match will burn down in moments and there is no second go.

Start with a surprise: wood does not burn. Not directly, anyway. The US Army's survival manual, FM 21-76, puts it plainly: fuel in a non-gaseous state does not burn directly.1 When you apply heat to it, it gives off a gas, and that gas, mixed with oxygen from the air, is what burns. The flames over a log are burning gas, not burning wood.

That is why the manual teaches the fire triangle. Its three sides are air, heat and fuel, and if you remove any one of them the fire goes out.2 Nearly every skill in this course supplies one side or takes one away on purpose: tinder is fuel that heats fast, a fire lay feeds in air, and banking or drowning a fire removes a side. The manual adds that the right ratio of the three matters, and that the only way to learn it is to practise.

People argued about what burning even is for a very long time. In the 1700s chemists explained it with phlogiston, a substance that burning things were supposed to release into the air. Antoine-Laurent Lavoisier, working with his collaborator and wife Marie-Anne Paulze Lavoisier, overturned that idea by showing that combustion and breathing both needed a newly isolated kind of air,3 which he named oxygen. One experiment that fed the debate came from Joseph Priestley, who heated a calx of mercury using a large burning lens:4 the sun is one of the oldest lighters of all.

concepts.title: In the field: the ten minutes before you strike
concepts.contentHtml:
The Army manual opens its fire chapter bluntly: in many survival situations, being able to start a fire can make the difference between living and dying.1 Fire warms you, cooks food, purifies water, sterilises bandages, signals for rescue and keeps animals at a distance, and the manual even counts the lift to your spirits. Hot food also saves the calories your body would otherwise spend making heat.2 So spend the first ten minutes getting ready, not striking.

  1. Decide why you need it. Warmth, cooking and signalling call for different fires. Weigh the terrain and weather, the materials around you and how much time you have.
  2. Choose the spot. Look for a dry place protected from the wind, sensibly placed for your shelter, with fuel nearby.
  3. Clear the ground. Scrape away brush and surface litter. The Army minimum is a circle at least 1 metre across;3 Smokey Bear's campfire guide asks for a 10-foot (3-metre) cleared circle,4 at least 15 feet (4.5 metres) from tents, plants and low branches.
  4. Gather all three piles first. Tinder, kindling and fuel, enough to keep the fire going as long as you need it, all within reach of where you will kneel.
  5. Light from the upwind side, so the breeze carries the flame into the tinder.
  6. Feed it, do not bury it. Fire needs air to grow, so add wood gradually rather than in a dense pile.5
Safety Check the local rules first: parks set their own, and Smokey Bear's advice is to skip the fire where it is banned or when conditions are dry or windy. Keep water and a shovel beside you and never leave a fire unattended. The Army manual also warns that fire can cause burns, and carbon monoxide poisoning when used in shelters.

concepts.title: Myth check: what actually burns
concepts.contentHtml:
Two beliefs trip up almost everyone on their first cold night.

Myth A log burns because the wood itself catches fire.
Reality Heat drives gas out of the wood, and it is that gas, mixed with oxygen, that burns.1 This is why a fat log will not light from a match: the little flame cannot heat it fast enough to give off much gas, while a curl of shaving thinner than paper can be heated through in a moment.
Myth Blowing on a tiny flame or a glowing spark will put it out.
Reality A hard gust can scatter it, but gentle air is food. When a spark has caught in tinder, the manual's instruction is to blow on it so it spreads and bursts into flame,2 and with a lens it says to gently blow or fan the smouldering tinder into flame. You are supplying the air side of the triangle.

Wait, really? You can watch the gas burn for yourself. In a course of lectures for young people at London's Royal Institution, Michael Faraday blew out a candle and showed the vapour rising from the wick. If he held a lighted taper two or three inches from the wick, a train of fire ran through the air until it reached the candle and lit it again.3 He told his audience that the heat is found where the air and the fuel come together, and that air is absolutely necessary for combustion, fresh air at that.4

title: Tinder, Kindling and Fuel
description: The three piles, why thin and dead catches first, and finding dry wood in the rain
tryIt: After rain, where collecting is allowed, split a thick dead stick and feel how much drier its core is than its bark.

concepts.title: How it works: thin, dead and dry
concepts.contentHtml:
It has rained for two days. Every stick you pick up is dark, cold and heavy with water, and your only hope is that something, somewhere, is still dry. Good news: something usually is, if you know where physics hides it.

A fire is built from three kinds of material, and the Army manual sorts them by how much heat they need. Tinder is dry material that ignites with little heat, so a spark can start it.1 Kindling is readily combustible material you add to burning tinder; it raises the fire's temperature until it can ignite the2 fuel, the less combustible material that burns slowly and steadily once lit. Smokey Bear's campfire guide gives a handy size rule: kindling is sticks smaller than 1 inch around.

Why does thin matter so much? Wildfire scientists class dead fuel by its timelag, the time a piece of a given size takes to get 63 per cent of the way to balance with the moisture around it.3 Grass and twigs less than a quarter of an inch (about 6 mm) thick are 1-hour fuels: they respond quickly to the weather, and their moisture swings greatly within a single day.4 Wood 3 to 6 inches thick is a 1,000-hour fuel, whose moisture follows a seven-day average of the weather. That slowness can work for you: after a shower, a thick dead branch may still be dry at its heart.

People who lived in wet places became masters of this. In 1890 Walter Hough of the US National Museum quoted the explorer James G. Swan, who called the Chinooks of the Columbia River the best wet-weather fire-makers he ever knew.5 They twirled a cedar stick between their palms into a hollow in a flat piece of the same wood, letting the sparks fall on finely frayed bark, and carried their fire-sticks with them, which improved with use.

concepts.title: In the field: finding dry fuel in the wet
concepts.contentHtml:
Start before you need it. The Army manual's advice is to collect kindling and tinder along the trail as you walk,1 and to keep the firewood dry.

  1. Look up, not down. Dry, standing dead wood and dry, dead branches still on the tree are your best bet. If you take sticks from the ground, pick ones not covered by leaves, which hold moisture.2
  2. Split it open. The inside of a thick dead branch or fallen trunk can be dry when the outside is soaked, and bark burns less well than the wood inside,3 so split or shave down to the pale core.
  3. Make tinder from what you find. The manual's list includes birch bark, shredded inner bark, fine wood shavings, dead grass and ferns, the fluffy seed heads of milkweed, dry cattails, bulrush or thistle,4 cotton, pocket lint and waxed paper.
  4. Sort three piles. Tinder, kindling and fuel, from finest to thickest. Make the tinder pile bigger than seems sensible.
  5. Dry what is damp. Once the fire is going, stack damp wood near it to dry, as hearth cooks did on rainy days when they piled wet wood around the back and sides of the fireplace.5
  6. Make char cloth in advance. Heat cotton cloth until it turns black without burning and keep it in an airtight container.6 It holds a spark for a long time, which makes it almost essential if all you have is a spark-maker.
Safety On a camping trip, follow the park's rules rather than the survival manual: collecting wood is not allowed in many US national parks, and Leave No Trace guidance is to use only dead wood already on the ground that you can break by hand.7 Never cut whole trees or branches, dead or alive: Smokey Bear points out that dead standing trees shelter birds and other wildlife. Shave wood with the blade moving away from you.

concepts.title: Myth check: wet wood and green wood
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth Wet wood never burns.
Reality Wet wood burns badly, not never. The National Park Service notes that wetter wood burns more slowly and smokes far more,1 and that wood which is too wet will not catch at all. Yet the Army manual says a tepee fire, whose outer sticks fall inward to feed the centre as it burns, works well even with wet wood.2 The secret is the order: dry tinder and dry kindling first, damp fuel only once the fire is hot, with more damp wood drying beside it.
Myth Green branches are free fuel: just snap some off a living tree.
Reality Smokey Bear's guide is blunt that live material won't burn.3 The Army manual is a little kinder, listing green wood as fuel only when it is finely split.4 Green leaves have a different job, which you will meet in the last lesson: making smoke.

Wait, really? Charring something can make it better at catching fire, and at resisting water. Hough described a Sitka fire set whose whole hearth had been charred, which, he wrote, repels moisture and also makes the wood easier to ignite.5 The same fire-makers frayed the bark of the arbor vitae for tinder and improved it by charring it slightly,6 though they preferred tinder made from a fungus because it was "quicker". Char cloth, the survival manual's favourite spark-catcher, is the same trick in cotton.

title: Spark and Ember
description: Matches, spark rods, flint and pyrite, the bow drill, and 400,000 years of making fire
tryIt: In a fire pit or on bare ground, strike a ferro rod with the back of a knife over a cotton-wool ball and count how many strikes it takes to get a flame.

concepts.title: How it works: a 400,000-year-old skill
concepts.contentHtml:
Your lighter clicks, sparks and gives you nothing: the fuel is gone. Fine. You are about to do what people managed long before anyone had a pocket to keep a lighter in.

Using fire and making it are different skills. A 2025 study in Nature sums up the long story: fire use developed over a million years, first harvesting natural fire, then keeping it going, and only then making it.1 Some of the oldest secure evidence of burning comes from Wonderwerk Cave in South Africa, where burned bone and ashed plant remains date to about a million years ago.2 That shows people living with fire, not lighting it.

The oldest evidence of actually making fire comes from Barnham, in Suffolk. On a 400,000-year-old buried land surface, archaeologists found heated sediments and fire-cracked flint handaxes beside two fragments of iron pyrite,3 a mineral later peoples struck against flint to make sparks. Pyrite is rare in that area, which suggests someone brought it there on purpose.4 Much later, around 50,000 years ago in France, Neanderthals left dozens of bifacial tools with polish and scratches matching experiments in which pyrite is struck at an angle against the tool to make fire,5 though the authors noted that whether Neanderthals made their fire or collected it from natural blazes was still a matter of debate.

Then there is Ötzi, the Iceman, who died in the Alps over 5,300 years ago. In his belt pouch were several pieces of fungus with traces of pyrite on them;6 the species is Fomes fomentarius. One of his flint tools also carries wear consistent with use as a strike-a-light. Striking flint with steel came later still: the method dates from the Iron Age and stayed among the most common ways to make fire until matches and lighters took over.7

concepts.title: In the field: from match to bow drill
concepts.contentHtml:
If you have a choice, carry fire rather than make it. The Army manual wants matches that are waterproof, stored in a waterproof container with a dependable striker.1 Spark rods work because certain alloys throw sparks when scraped: in a patent filed in 1903, Carl Auer von Welsbach reported that the rare earth metal cerium becomes pyrophoric when alloyed with iron,2 with the best results at about 30 per cent iron. A lens from binoculars, a camera or a magnifying glass works too, but only on bright, sunny days.3 When all of that is gone, there is the bow drill.

  1. Make the set. A straight, seasoned hardwood drill about 2 cm thick and 25 cm long;4 a seasoned softwood fire board about 2.5 cm thick and 10 cm wide; a socket of stone, hardwood or bone to press on the drill; and a bow of springy green wood with any cord tied tight.
  2. Cut the board. Make a small depression about 2 cm from one edge, then a V-shaped cut from the edge into it.
  3. Set the tinder. Lay the fire first, then put a bundle of tinder under the V and one foot on the board.
  4. Drill. Loop the string over the drill, seat it in the depression, press down with the socket and saw the bow back and forth. Once the motion is smooth, press harder and go faster.
  5. Nurse the ember. The drill grinds hot black powder into the tinder until a spark catches.5 Blow on the tinder until it bursts into flame.
Safety Never pour petrol or other fuels on a fire to help it along. The National Park Service warns that even lighter fluid squirted onto embers or open flames can flare up and burn your skin.6 Aim a spark rod's sparks down into the tinder, away from people, and keep a lens in its case when you are not using it.

concepts.title: Myth check: two sticks and old matches
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth Just rub two sticks together.
Reality It is a skill, not a trick, and the sources pull two ways. In Tahiti during the Beagle voyage, Charles Darwin watched his guides make a light by rubbing a blunt pointed stick in a groove made in another, in a few seconds.1 When he tried, it took the greatest exertion before, to his great pride, he ignited the dust.2 The Army manual calls friction methods exhausting and says they need practice. Yet Walter Hough called the idea that friction fire is very difficult a prevalent belief, and wrote that he had repeatedly made fire in thirty seconds by twirling sticks and in five seconds with a bow drill.3 Both are true: with the right wood and practice it is quick; without them it is misery.
Myth Matches only go back to the 1800s.
Reality Friction matches do, but the idea is older. Sticks coated with a chemical mixture were used to start fires in 577 during a siege in northern China, but the technique was lost.4 The friction match proper came from John Walker, a chemist in Stockton-on-Tees, whose paste-covered stick caught fire when he scraped it on his hearth in 1826–27;5 by 1827 he was selling "friction lights", and he never patented them.

Wait, really? Darwin also carried some early "promethean" matches, which he lit by biting. It was thought so wonderful that a man could strike fire with his teeth that whole families gathered to watch,6 and he was once offered a dollar for a single match.

title: Fire Lays, Rain and Wind
description: Tepee, lean-to, log cabin and pyramid lays, the Dakota fire hole, and fire in wind and snow
tryIt: In a permitted fire pit, build a pyramid fire, light it on top and time how long it burns before you need to touch it.

concepts.title: How it works: building for air
concepts.contentHtml:
The rain has eased, but the wind has not. You have tinder, kindling and a sad heap of damp branches, and you will get one good flame. How you stack the wood decides whether that flame grows or dies.

A fire lay is a little machine for moving air and heat. Kindling raises the fire's temperature until it can ignite less combustible fuel,1 so each layer must sit where the flames below will reach it, with gaps for air to flow in. The Army manual's cross-ditch lay shows the idea at its simplest: you scratch a cross about 30 cm across and 7.5 cm deep, put tinder in the middle, and the shallow ditch lets air sweep under the tinder to give the fire a draught.2

Wind is both friend and enemy. Choose a spot protected from it, and the manual suggests a fire wall of logs or rocks that reflects heat where you want it, reduces flying sparks and cuts down the wind blowing into the fire. Then it adds a warning: you still need enough wind to keep the fire burning.3 Smokey Bear's campfire guide asks for a flat spot with open sky above, away from gusty winds and open fields.4

Hearth cooks knew all this by feel. The National Park Service's Fort Scott historic site explains how a cook built a fire on andirons over old ashes and coals, leaving a one-inch space so air could circulate,5 and chose the split of the wood for the job: pieces split into quarters burn rapidly, giving the flames needed for roasting, while small pieces split only in half burn more slowly with less flame.6

concepts.title: In the field: four lays and a hole
concepts.contentHtml:
Four classic lays and one hole in the ground, from the Army manual and Smokey Bear's campfire guide. Choose by weather and by job: a quick hot fire for cooking, a slow one for the night.

  1. Tepee. Arrange tinder and kindling in a cone and light the centre. As it burns, the outer sticks fall inward and feed it, which is why it copes with wet wood. Smokey Bear rates it, with the lean-to, as best for cooking.
  2. Lean-to. Push a green stick into the ground at about 30 degrees, its end pointing in the direction of the wind, as the manual puts it.1 Place tinder deep underneath, lean kindling against the stick, light the tinder and add more kindling as it catches.
  3. Log cabin. Surround the tinder with kindling stacked at right angles, topped with the smallest pieces:2 Smokey Bear's pick for a long-lasting campfire.
  4. Pyramid. Lay two small logs parallel, cover them with a solid layer of small logs laid across, then add three or four more layers, each smaller and at right angles to the one below. Make a starter fire on top. The manual says it burns downward and needs no attention during the night.3
  5. Dakota fire hole. Dig a hole for the fire and, on its upwind side, a second hole joined to it for air.4 It hides the flame and is good for cooking.
  6. On snow or soaked ground, build a platform first: lay green logs side by side, add one or two more layers, and set the top layer crosswise to the one below.5
Safety Use an existing fire ring where there is one, and keep the Dakota hole for real need, since Leave No Trace guidance is not to dig trenches. Keep spare wood stacked upwind of the fire so a sudden breeze cannot light it.6 Remember that synthetic clothing melts when it gets hot, so keep fleece away from sparks.

concepts.title: Myth check: river stones and upside-down fires
concepts.contentHtml:
Fire lays attract folklore. Here are two beliefs worth testing before you rely on them.

Myth Smooth stones from a stream make the perfect fire ring.
Reality The Army manual's caution is blunt: do not use wet or porous rocks, because they may explode when heated.1 Stones from a stream are wet by definition. Use dry, solid stones, or better still, an existing fire ring or a metal one.
Myth You always light a fire at the bottom.
Reality The manual's pyramid lay is lit on top. You make a starter fire on the top layer, and as it burns it ignites the logs below it, one layer at a time.2 The result is a fire that burns downward for hours without being touched, which is why the survival manual likes it for a night in the open. On a campsite the Park Service rule still wins: never go to sleep while a fire is too hot to touch.

Wait, really? The Army manual recommends a fire wall to cut the wind, then warns in the next breath that you still need enough wind to keep the fire burning. The Dakota fire hole solves both problems at once. The fire sits below ground, concealed,3 while the second hole dug on the upwind side gives it a steady supply of air. The manual likes it for cooking, too, and the hole keeps the glow out of sight.

title: Keeping and Using Fire
description: Banking and carrying embers, boiling water, signal fires and smoke, and putting a fire out cold
tryIt: Next time you put out a campfire, drown it, stir it, drown it again and then hover the back of your hand over the ashes to check they are cold.

concepts.title: How it works: keeping fire alive
concepts.contentHtml:
You did it. The fire is crackling, your fingers have feeling again, and now comes the part nobody warns you about: you have to keep it all night, and perhaps carry it tomorrow.

Keeping fire is older than making it. The Barnham study describes fire use developing from harvesting natural fire to maintaining it, and only then to making it, so tending a fire is the oldest fire skill there is. The trick is to starve the fire without killing it. Coals buried under dirt or sand are insulated, and the National Park Service warns that this can keep them hot even longer than if they were left exposed. That is what banking exploits: the Army manual's advice is to bank the fire to keep the coals alive overnight,1 and the hearth cooks at Fort Scott banked theirs each night for the next morning's use.2 Hardwoods, the same page notes, give a good supply of red-hot coals.

To travel with fire, people carried it smouldering. Ötzi had two birch-bark containers, and the interior of one was blackened and held freshly picked Norway maple leaves and fragments of charcoal.3 The museum that keeps him thinks he wrapped embers in the leaves, which could keep them for several hours and be fanned into fire in a few seconds.4 Hough described a Quinault fire set from Washington Territory with a slow-match of braided cedar bark that was often carried for weeks, held under a blanket against wind and rain.5 The Army manual's version is shorter: carry lighted punk, the rotten wood of dead logs, whenever you can.

concepts.title: In the field: water, signals and a cold finish
concepts.contentHtml:
A fire that is burning well is a tool. After warmth, its most useful jobs are making water safe and getting you found, and its last job, the one you must never skip, is going out completely.

  1. Boil your water. If it is cloudy, filter it through a clean cloth or let it settle and draw off the clear water. Bring it to a rolling boil for 1 minute1 (3 minutes above 6,500 feet, about 2,000 metres), let it cool and store it covered. Boiling cannot make water containing fuel or toxic chemicals safe.2
  2. Signal at night with fire. Three fires in a triangle are the international distress signal; a straight line of three, about 25 metres apart, also works. Build them early and keep them protected until you need them. If you are alone and cannot keep three going, keep one.
  3. Signal by day with smoke. Three columns of smoke also mean distress. Make the smoke contrast with the background: smother a large fire with green leaves, moss or a little water for white smoke, or add rubber or oil-soaked rags for black.
  4. Put it out cold. Drown it with water until the hissing stops.3 Stir the water into the embers with a shovel and scrape the sticks and logs. Drown it again. Then feel, holding the back of your hand over the ashes. Leave No Trace adds: burn wood and coals to ash where you can, and scatter the cool ashes.
Safety Never take a fire, a barbecue or a camp stove into a tent or a house. Carbon monoxide has no colour or smell;4 the CDC warns never to burn charcoal or use a portable gas camp stove indoors, and never to run a generator inside, even with doors and windows open. Burning anything but wood, especially plastic, can release toxic gases,5 so stay upwind of signal smoke. If a fire escapes, call the emergency services straight away and give your location.

concepts.title: Myth check: dirt, ashes and invisible heat
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth Kick dirt over a campfire and it is out.
Reality Dirt and sand can insulate the coals, banking them and keeping them hot even longer than if they were left exposed.1 Smokey Bear's guide says not to put out a fire with just dirt or sand. If you truly have no water, the Park Service's fallback is to spread the coals out and keep stirring dirt and sand among them until they are out.
Myth No flames and no red glow means it is safe to leave.
Reality Whitish or grey coals can keep their heat for hours and flare up if the wind starts gusting.2 Smokey Bear's rule is to scrape and stir until no embers are exposed or smouldering, not just the red ones,3 and the Park Service's test is simple: if the fire is too hot to touch, do not leave or go to sleep.

Wait, really? Banking a fire on purpose and failing to put one out are the same physics: a blanket of ash or dirt holds the heat in and lets the coals smoulder on. That is why abandoned campfires matter. Nearly 85 per cent of wildland fires in the United States are caused by people,4 according to National Park Service figures for 2000 to 2017, and campfires left unattended are on its list of causes,5 alongside burning debris, equipment, discarded cigarettes and arson.
